title: Synagogues, Study Houses, and Hasidic Life in Łuków
summary: The book repeatedly returns to prayer, study, rabbis, and Hasidic practice as foundations of Łuków’s Jewish identity.
editorialContent:
## A town gathered around its houses of prayer

In the memorial book’s recollection, religious life in Łuków did not revolve around one congregation alone. It occupied a landscape of large and small institutions: the [Great Synagogue](/communities/lukow/records/mention_2e31aefbcf02758dd4ec17b1), the old and new bet midrash, neighborhood prayer rooms, Hasidic shtiblach, and schools where children and young men studied. The book describes these places as both houses of worship and settings for learning, communal decisions, charity, and daily companionship.

One witness, Shimen Siruke, remembered the town’s older worshippers gathering in the *shul-hoyf*—the synagogue courtyard—at the [Great Synagogue of Łuków](/communities/lukow/records/mention_e0eb1dbc391387851d8dbc93) and the Old Beth Midrash. He associated these institutions with Ashkenazi worship and the town’s established religious leadership. The Great Synagogue, he wrote, held hundreds of worshippers and was “the splendor of the city.” Painters [Hersh Lieber](/communities/lukow/records/mention_c13eeebab08bfa49bf6e8f3b) and [Chaim Mates Mandelbaum](/communities/lukow/records/mention_e1fb8e3df434f4d04bd8d72a) decorated it. The [Talmud Torah](/communities/lukow/records/mention_ed7edbb615c430cf0eed0122) stood next door, making education part of the same communal precinct.

That picture is one of remembered religious life, not a complete architectural inventory. The independent Virtual Shtetl account places Łuków’s synagogue, bet midrash, and mikveh in the historic Jewish quarter and gives street locations for several prayer houses. It also notes that many records documenting the community’s early history have not survived. The site’s entries identify buildings on Browarna, Bożnicza, and Staropijarska streets, but they do not establish that every name used in the memorial book corresponds neatly to a specific surviving structure or address. [Virtual Shtetl’s history of Łuków](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/99-history/137635-history-of-community) and [its listing of synagogues and prayer houses](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/112-synagogues-houses-of-prayer-and-others) add a topographical frame to the book’s intimate recollections.

## Study, teaching, and care for the poor

Learning took place in several settings. At the Great Synagogue, a group gathered each evening around a long table to study with [Ephraim Lichtenberg](/communities/lukow/records/mention_e51b6789ad14792f7b3bdce7). In the smaller study house, carters, butchers, and craftsmen prayed and studied between afternoon and evening prayers and on Saturday afternoons with [Aaron Mikra-Rabbi](/communities/lukow/records/mention_e3f7b1e5ddba174948c5225c). The distinction was not simply between prayer and study: work, worship, and learning shared the same rooms and rhythms.

The [Old Beth Midrash](/communities/lukow/records/mention_509cb7451d47c2b669d18dfc) served an even wider range of needs. The book recalls sermons, debates, elections, and, during the First World War, the organization of assistance for refugees. It also remembers [Ephraim Mezritcher](/communities/lukow/records/mention_176ac1d036aac80dc5696a61) teaching poor Jews there on Saturday afternoons. Such recollections show a study house not as an isolated schoolroom but as an institution that could become a civic meeting place and emergency shelter.

The [Łuków Yeshiva](/communities/lukow/records/mention_faae04234b5a29afdeed18a0) operated in a bet midrash, drawing students from the town and beyond. The memorial book names Rabbi Getzel Manish as its leader and recalls teachers Leibish, Velvel, Benzion, Chaim Yidel, and Levi. Another passage calls the municipal yeshiva the “Hok,” or House of Study, and names R. Getzel Lempiter (Menishes) as its spiritual head. The accounts preserve overlapping names and descriptions, but do not make every identification or institutional title entirely clear; it is safer to retain those differences than to assume they refer to precisely the same person or arrangement.

The community-supported Talmud Torah served children whose families could not afford private instruction. Siruke remembered a committee of *gabbaim* raising money for teachers’ salaries and insisted that poor children’s education mattered to the whole town. The wider historical account confirms the importance of communal education, while distinguishing institutions not always differentiated in the memorial narrative: Virtual Shtetl reports private *hederim*, at least two Talmud Torah schools connected to the community, and a Mizrachi school. That broader list suggests a more varied educational landscape than any single witness could describe. [Virtual Shtetl on Łuków’s community institutions](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/99-history/137635-historia-spolecznosci)

## Hasidic prayer houses and distinct affiliations

Alongside the older communal synagogue and study houses stood prayer rooms organized around Hasidic affiliations. The memorial book names the [Gerer Shtibl](/communities/lukow/records/mention_cce8b4b592272a187c998ed4) and the [Mezritcher Shtibl](/communities/lukow/records/mention_c35ed3840af0065b189c7e3a), and recalls a debate among Hasidim in Łuków. Its account of a newer study house, the [Chaya Sarah Study House](/communities/lukow/records/mention_a10fbb57c56691566da3b4f4), associates it with [Chaya Sarah](/communities/lukow/records/mention_1a09673555473a05d078ea40) and with well-to-do householders including [Moses Lichtenstein](/communities/lukow/records/mention_7bd427277d6dcbaac3c33e55), [Moses Barnstein](/communities/lukow/records/mention_2f5e90dbeff26643bf646b91), and [Eliezer Wachsman](/communities/lukow/records/mention_34d2f9e0ceed3e561a41a3a5). The records also connect [Zevulun Aryeh](/communities/lukow/records/mention_ed7edbb615c430cf0eed0122) with the Talmud Torah and Mezritcher Shtibl, and [Berl Yisrael Itzhaks](/communities/lukow/records/mention_0e4d475f62066578f1bb4fea) with the latter.

Siruke’s broader account names followers of Gur, Kotzk, Aleksander, Porisov, Modzitz, Radzyń, Sochaczew, and Lublin, among others. He recalled that people traveled to Hasidic courts for holidays to gather around their rebbes and hear them teach. The independent Virtual Shtetl history likewise identifies shtiblach associated with Kock, Radzyń, Aleksandrów Łódzki, and Góra Kalwaria, and describes the establishment in Łuków of Hersz Morgenstern’s court in 1906. These accounts broadly agree that Łuków’s Hasidic life was plural, not the preserve of one court. The exact relationship between every named local shtibl and a particular rebbe or court remains a promising subject for further research: [Hasidic courts represented in Łuków](research:Which Hasidic courts had shtiblach in Łuków, and when?).

The memorial book also gives glimpses of named local figures without always supplying biographies. [Gershon Flug](/communities/lukow/records/mention_e8953abb1988b4d7dce5b5e3) is remembered as the cantor who began Kol Nidrei. The prominence of a cantor in a recollection of the synagogue’s services hints at the importance of sound and ritual alongside study, but the account does not provide enough detail to reconstruct his life or career.

## Rabbis, communal authority, and a changing town

The book places rabbis within this network of institutions, teaching, prayer, and communal authority. One passage says that the rabbi known by the acronym [Bach](/communities/lukow/records/mention_c06436dc20f5227ef1820926) served in Łuków, while another associates the Bach with several communities and the Council of the Four Lands. The book itself leaves the acronym unexpanded. Without independent evidence establishing the identity, it should remain an attribution to the memorial text rather than a confidently identified biography.

Religious life was not separate from public affairs. Study houses hosted meetings and debates; communal organizations raised funds and managed schools; and arguments over leadership could become intensely political. The book remembers Agudah’s role in communal life, while the independent historical account describes a town with multiple political and cultural currents, including Agudat Yisrael and Zionist, Bundist, and communist activity. [Yad Vashem’s Łuków entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529) likewise describes interwar Jewish life as institutionally and politically varied. That evidence is a useful check on any impression that shared religious institutions meant uniform beliefs or politics.

The geography and practices remembered here belonged to a living community, not merely a collection of buildings. The [Łuków Jewish community](/communities/lukow/records/mention_f24bb37493b0a89d690f2483) gathered for prayer, study, teaching, charity, and argument across institutions that could be both distinct and connected. The book’s recollections preserve the people who animated those places; outside records help locate some buildings and show the wider institutional variety, but cannot replace the local testimony. The memorial account describes residents fleeing during the wartime bombing and returning to years of persecution and destruction. Yad Vashem’s account provides the wider chronology of occupation and the community’s wartime fate. Together, they mark the rupture that ended the world these witnesses remembered.
